text: Lucy Weston Pickett (January 19, 1904 – November 23, 1997) was a Mary Lyon Professor and Camille and Henry Dreyfus Chair in Chemistry at Mount Holyoke College. She was born in Beverly, Massachusetts, to Lucy Weston, a former school teacher and elementary school principal, and George Ernest Pickett, a former seaman, and had one brother, Thomas Austin Pickett, who also became a chemist. Both Lucy and Thomas pursued similar academic and professional paths while maintaining a close relationship. Pickett attended high school in Beverly and entered Mount Holyoke College in South Hadley, Massachusetts, in 1921, graduating in 1925 with summa cum laude in both chemistry and mathematics. She double majored in chemistry and mathematics and earned a master's degree in two years before moving to the University of Illinois, where she completed her Ph.D. in analytical chemistry with minors in physical chemistry and physics. Her dissertation research focused on the effects of X-rays on chemical reactions and the X-ray structures of organic compounds. Pickett taught at the University of Illinois and Goucher College before returning to Mount Holyoke in 1930, where she remained until her retirement in 1968. During her 1932–1933 leave, she worked with Sir William Bragg, the famous X-ray crystallographer and Nobel laureate, at the Royal Institution, London. In 1939, she received an Educational Foundation Fellowship to work with Victor Henri at the University of Liège, Belgium, and with George Kistiakowsky at Harvard. In 1942, she and Emma Perry Carr traveled to Chicago to attend a spectroscopy conference organized by Robert S. Mulliken. In 1952, Pickett collaborated with Mulliken on theoretical interpretations of the spectrum of the benzenium ion. She joined an active research team at Mount Holyoke that included Emma Perry Carr and Mary Sherrill, focusing on molecular structures through spectroscopy. Her colleagues and students established the Lucy Pickett Lectureship to bring outstanding speakers to the campus; the first speaker was Robert Mulliken, the 1966 Chemistry Nobel laureate, with whom Pickett had published a paper in 1954. In the 1970s, Pickett requested that the funds be used to honor women scientists. Her research on X-ray crystallography and ultraviolet absorption spectroscopy of organic molecules received numerous honors and was supported by grants from the Office of Naval Research, the National Science Foundation, and the Petroleum Research Fund of the American Chemical Society.
